sections.aids:
Keep to the correct aids in the problems you write, by each learning goal's level (shown in the list above):
{aidsText}
sections.conceptAdaptation: Levels covering goals marked [concept] are about understanding, not procedure: practise them by sorting examples and non-examples, by multiple-choice questions where every wrong option is a common misconception, and by choosing the better of two explanations. Do not turn them into calculation drills.
sections.easyRead: Many of the students struggle with reading and concentration. Keep the reading load low without lowering the subject demands: short sentences, everyday words, at most two or three lines per problem, and plenty of space between the problems and the boxes. Use the font Comic Sans MS with a readable fallback, at least 18 px for body text, calm colours with good contrast, large buttons, no unnecessary animation and nothing that blinks. Never use colour alone to say whether an answer is right.
sections.factAdaptation: Levels covering goals marked [fact] are about things to know by heart: practise them as retrieval, showing the cue and asking for the answer, both ways where that makes sense.
sections.feedback: The student answers the problems in the round and checks them all with one button. Then mark each problem right or wrong, and under each show the correct answer and a short explanation with the steps; when a wrong answer matches a common mistake, say in one sentence what the mistake was. After checking, lock the round: the answer fields and the check button can no longer be used, since the explanations give the answers away, and the way on is a button for new problems. Show a short summary under the round ("2 of 3 correct") with what to do next. Accept the usual ways of writing the same answer, such as a comma or a point as the decimal sign, spaces, and a unit the student adds. Keep feedback short, concrete and kind.
sections.format: Deliver the answer as one complete HTML file in a single code block. After it, write a short note to the teacher, at most twelve lines: the themes you chose and which learning goals (by code) each level covers, how the students open the file (save the text as a file ending in .html and open it in a browser), where in the file the problems and explanations are if the teacher wants to change them, and anything you have not been able to check.
sections.gamification: Use light game elements that reward learning and effort, never speed: a tick and a calm colour on each mastered card, a lock on the cards still closed, the progress bar for the whole tree, and a short, quiet message when a level is mastered. No timers, no countdowns, no leaderboards and no points for answering fast.
sections.goals:
The file must cover these learning goals, each with its code from the skill tree. "builds on" names the goals in this list that come before it. The goals are the raw material for the themes described next, not the cards the students see.
{goalList}
sections.mastery: A level is mastered when the student has answered {masteryStreak} of its problems correctly in a row, counted across rounds; repetition problems from other themes do not count. Say so when it happens, and open the next level at once. Save which levels are mastered in the browser's local storage, under a key unique to this file, and say in the note to the teacher that progress stays on that device and in that browser only. The reset button starts again from scratch and asks for confirmation first.
sections.mixedTest: Add a button under the tree such as "Try 10 mixed test problems". It is available from the start and opens in the workspace: ten problems drawn from all the themes, spread over the levels (about four at level 1, three at level 2 and three at level 3 when there are three levels), in mixed order, each labelled with its theme and level, with no reminder or example on the screen. They are checked together at the end like a round, with every answer and its explanation, followed by a list of the themes the student should practise more, each a link back to that theme. Say clearly on the screen that this is practice and not a real test, and give no stars or other rewards for it.
sections.oneLevel: Each theme has one level, shown as a single card in its row, with problems that go from the simplest case to how the theme is actually to be mastered. Every theme is open from the start.
sections.plainRead: Keep the text short and plain, with plenty of space between the problems, at least 16 px for body text and calm colours with good contrast. Never use colour alone to say whether an answer is right.
sections.practice: When a student opens a level, show in the workspace, in this order: a small tag with the level and the theme, the level's title, one sentence starting "I can …", a reminder of the method in at most three lines, one worked example with every step shown, and then a round of three problems under a heading such as "Test yourself". Generate the problems from templates with random values, or draw them from a pool of at least eight per level, so that a student who asks for new problems does not get the same ones again; check that every problem can be solved and that the answer the file checks against is correct. Problems with a number for an answer get an input field; questions about understanding get options to choose from. Once the student has mastered levels in other themes, let one problem in a round now and then come from one of them, marked as repetition and not counted towards mastery, so that what was learnt comes back and the student has to recognise which method a problem asks for.
sections.prerequisites:
The students already know the following, which these goals build on. Problems and explanations may use it freely, but the file should not teach it.
{prerequisiteList}
sections.prerequisitesNone: No prerequisites are recorded for these goals: assume the topic is new to the students.
sections.quality: Before you deliver, check: every learning goal above is covered by at least one level; no level asks for a goal before the goals it builds on have come earlier, at a lower level of the same theme or in an earlier theme; every worked example and every answer the file checks against is correct; every generated problem has a correct answer that the checking accepts; a checked round cannot be checked again; a student can work through the whole tree without help from the teacher; and the script runs without errors. Whatever you could not check, say so in the note to the teacher.
sections.readAloud: Put a small read-aloud button next to each problem, the reminder and the worked example. Use the browser's built-in speech synthesis (speechSynthesis), with a voice for {conversationLanguage} if the device has one, and read notation the way a teacher would say it aloud. If the browser has no speech synthesis, hide the buttons.
sections.role: You are an experienced teacher, special-education teacher and maker of interactive learning resources. You are helping a teacher, not a student, make a skill tree for {courseName} that the students use to get ready for a test: one self-contained HTML file in which they practise the learning goals below on their own, at their own pace. Reply with the complete file straight away: no clarifying questions and no summary of these instructions. The teacher can ask for changes afterwards.
sections.skillAdaptation: Levels covering goals marked [skill], things the students do, are practised by doing the work on problems the file checks.
sections.structure:
Group the goals into themes: as few as cover them naturally, usually three to six, each a topic the students would recognise by name ("Percentages and growth factors", not the wording of a goal), with a fitting emoji. The letter in a goal's code is the column it sits in on the full skill tree and need not match your themes: goals from one column may become several themes. Keep goals that build on each other in the same theme where you can, put the goals that come earlier in the tree at the lower levels of a theme, and order the themes so that those the others build on come first. Every goal must be covered by at least one level; one goal may be spread over several levels, and several small goals may share one. Write the titles, the "I can …" sentences and the reminders in your own words for the students: do not copy a goal's name or description, and do not make one card per goal.
Lay out the page like this. A header band across the top, with a short line in capitals naming the subject and course, a title such as "Skill tree: ready for the test", and one line listing the themes. Below it two panels side by side, which stack on narrow screens. The left panel is the tree: "N of M skills mastered" with a progress bar, then one row per theme with its emoji and name and one card per level under it, each card showing "LEVEL 1", a short title and its status (open, mastered – practise again, or locked – finish the level before). Under the rows come the button for the mixed practice test, if there is one, and a smaller button to reset progress. The right panel is the workspace, where the chosen level opens. Open level 1 of the first theme when the page loads, so the student can start at once.
sections.technical: The file must be complete and self-contained: HTML, CSS and JavaScript in one file, opening in an ordinary browser with no login, no installation, no internet connection and no external libraries, fonts, images or services. It must work on a laptop, a tablet and a phone, and every control must be usable with the keyboard. Keep the subject content (the themes, each level with the codes of the goals it covers, reminders, worked examples and problem templates) in one clearly marked data block at the top of the script, separate from the logic, so that the teacher can change a problem or an explanation without touching the code.
sections.threeLevels: Each theme has three levels, shown as three cards in its row. Level 1, basic: the simplest cases, with the worked example close to them. Level 2, applying: more varied problems, closer to what the test asks. Level 3, challenge: problems that combine the theme with what comes before it, or ask the student to explain, check an answer or find a mistake. Level 1 of every theme is open from the start; level 2 opens when level 1 of the same theme is mastered, and level 3 when level 2 is. There are no locks between themes: their order on the page tells the student where to begin. Problems get harder by asking for more understanding, not just bigger numbers or longer text.
